opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The readings today left me with more questions than answers.

God commanded Jeremiah to speak every word He gave him, without omission. Jeremiah obeyed. The House of Judah wanted to omit not only his words, but Jeremiah himself. They wanted him put to death because the truth he spoke was too difficult to hear.

Then in the Gospel, Jesus returns to His own hometown. The people ask, "Where did He get such wisdom?" "Is He not the carpenter's son?" They cannot see beyond what is familiar. They become offended, and because of their lack of faith, few mighty works are done there.

The prophets were rejected. Jesus was rejected. Yet Jesus accomplished what the prophets before Him never could. Everything they proclaimed for centuries found its fulfillment in Him. They pointed toward the promise. He was the Promise.

Now it is centuries later, and the world is filled with religions, teachers, prophets, and countless ways of searching for God.

I was born into the Catholic faith. It is the home where I learned to know God, where Scripture began to make sense, where the sacraments gave life to what I believed. I follow it wholeheartedly, not because I was simply born into it, but because over time I have found its teachings to ring true within my heart.

Still, I meet people from other faiths who are just as devoted to what they practice. They, too, are searching. I do not like saying one religion is truer than another as though I can see into another person's soul. I believe there is one God. I also believe that every human heart longs for Him, whether it recognizes that longing or not.

Perhaps that longing is exactly what God placed within us.

I wonder why there were prophets before Christ, yet no prophets after Him in the same way. Jesus fulfilled the Father's promise. He does not need someone to complete what He began. Yet people still arise claiming new revelations, new paths, new truths. Why are we always searching? Is it because we have not yet learned to rest? Is it because our hearts continue reaching for the One they were made for, sometimes in the right places and sometimes in the wrong ones?

I do not think God is trying to confuse us. I think He knows us. He knows how easily we wander, how often we mistake our own voices for His, how desperately we seek meaning. Perhaps He is more patient than I can imagine.

It saddens me to read Matthew's Gospel and watch Jesus be restrained by His own people. They knew His family. They knew His trade. Yet they could not know Him. How often do we still do the same? We reduce God to what we think we already understand and miss what He is doing before our very eyes.

Humans seem to run in every direction. We wound one another. We reject truth when it challenges us. We spend our lives searching while the One we seek continues calling us.

How long, Lord? How long until suffering ends? Why must the refinement continue? Why can't we simply enter Your Kingdom now?

Then I remember the potter from yesterday's reading. The vessel was not finished because the potter was not finished shaping it.  In fact, as an amateur potter, a piece is seldom perfectly done.  It just gets close to good enough.  

Maybe that is where I find myself today—not with answers, but still on the wheel.

Lord, I do not ask You to end the questions. I ask You to keep me in Your hands until the day You finish what You have begun.
